q: What is Figure A that is an instrument used in surveying to measure horizontal and vertical angles with precision?
n: A theodolite is an optical instrument for measuring horizontal and vertical angles precisely in surveying and layout. A total station adds electronic distance measurement. Source: Surveying references (e.g., Wolf and Ghilani, Elementary Surveying).

q: What is Figure B that is a pointed weight suspended from a string, used to establish a true vertical reference line?
n: A plumb bob is a pointed weight hung on a string. Gravity makes the string truly vertical, giving a plumb reference. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; surveying references.

q: What is Figure C that is a tool containing a liquid-filled vial with a bubble, used to check if surfaces are level or plumb?
n: A spirit level has a liquid-filled glass vial with an air bubble. When the bubble is centered, the surface is level or plumb. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; carpentry references.

q: What is Figure D that is a heavy construction machine with a boom, stick, bucket, and cab used for digging and earth-moving?
n: An excavator has a boom, a stick (arm) and a bucket mounted on a cab that rotates 360° on tracks or wheels. It is used for digging and earthmoving. Source: Peurifoy, Construction Planning, Equipment and Methods.

q: What is Figure E that is a temporary framework set up to mark building corners and levels during excavation and layout?
n: Batter boards are horizontal boards on stakes set outside the building corners. String lines stretched between them mark the wall lines and levels during excavation. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (site layout).

q: Which excavating machine has a digging bucket on a two-part articulated arm, usually mounted at the rear of a tractor or front loader?
n: A backhoe has a digging bucket on a two-part articulated arm (boom and dipper) at the rear of a tractor, usually with a front loader bucket, so it is called a backhoe loader. Source: Peurifoy, Construction Planning, Equipment and Methods.

q: Which heavy equipment clears vegetation and pushes large volumes of soil during site preparation?
n: A bulldozer is a tracked tractor with a front blade that clears vegetation and pushes large volumes of soil during site preparation. Source: Peurifoy, Construction Planning, Equipment and Methods.

q: Which equipment is best for leveling and grading large areas of land during site development?
n: A motor grader has a long adjustable blade between its axles. It fine-levels and shapes large areas and roadbeds to grade. Source: Peurifoy, Construction Planning, Equipment and Methods.

q: Which machine compacts soil, gravel or asphalt before construction?
n: Road rollers (smooth drum, vibratory or pneumatic) compact soil, aggregate base and asphalt layers to the required density. Source: Peurifoy, Construction Planning, Equipment and Methods; DPWH Standard Specifications Item 104.

q: Which equipment is designed for digging deep, narrow trenches for pipes and cables?
n: A trencher uses a digging chain or wheel to cut deep, narrow trenches for pipes and cables quickly. Source: Peurifoy, Construction Planning, Equipment and Methods.

q: What should be done first, before setting up batter boards and staking?
o: Verify that the boundary monuments are in the correct position
Build workers' quarters and material storage
n: All layout starts from the property lines, so the boundary monuments must be verified by a geodetic engineer before any batter boards or stakes are set. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (site layout); PD 1096 permit requirements (lot survey).

q: Where should excavation begin?
o: At the rear portion of the property
n: Excavation usually begins at the rear of the property, so the cut and spoil do not block site access, materials can come in from the front and the work moves toward the street. Source: Philippine construction field practice; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: On a sloping job site, where should excavation begin?
o: At the sides of the lot
n: On a sloping site, excavation starts at the lowest elevation so rain and groundwater drain out of the work instead of ponding in the cut. Source: Peurifoy, Construction Planning, Equipment and Methods.

q: When is "lason" (soil poisoning) applied?
n: "Lason" is soil poisoning: a termiticide applied to the soil under slabs and around foundations when termites are present or expected. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (soil treatment); FPA-registered termiticide labels.

q: How is backfill material commonly estimated on site?
n: Backfill is a volume quantity, estimated in cubic meters of compacted fill (with an allowance for loose-to-compacted shrinkage). Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (earthworks); DPWH Standard Specifications Item 104.

q: What is Figure A that is a brick laid with its long face parallel to the wall and its longest dimension horizontal, commonly used in standard brick bonding patterns?
n: A stretcher is laid flat with its long face showing along the wall. It is the basic unit of running bond. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (brick positions).

q: What is Figure B that is a brick laid flat with its short end exposed on the face of the wall, providing structural bonding between wythes?
n: A header is laid flat with its short end exposed. It spans across the wall thickness and ties the wythes together. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (brick positions).

q: What is Figure C that is a brick laid horizontally on the longer edge with the shorter end exposed, often used for sills or caps?
n: A rowlock is laid on its long narrow edge with the end exposed. It is used for sills, caps and arches. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (brick positions).

q: What is Figure D that is a brick laid vertically with its long, narrow face showing on the wall’s surface, commonly used for decorative courses or lintels?
n: A soldier stands upright on its end with the narrow long face showing. It is used for decorative courses and over openings. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (brick positions).

q: What is Figure E that is a brick laid vertically with its broadest face showing on the wall's surface, creating a distinct pattern?
n: A sailor stands upright with its broad face exposed. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (brick positions).

q: Why is CHB the most commonly used masonry unit in the Philippines?
n: CHB dominates Philippine construction because it is made everywhere from local cement and sand, is cheap and needs only basic skills. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (masonry); DTI-BPS PNS 16 (CHB standard).

q: Which is NOT a common CHB size?
n: Local CHB is made in 4" (100 mm), 6" (150 mm) and 8" (200 mm) thicknesses, all 8" × 16" (200 × 400 mm) in face size. A 5" block is not standard. Source: PNS 16:1994 (concrete hollow blocks); Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: How many cells does a standard CHB have?
n: The standard Philippine CHB has three cells, which take the vertical bars and the grout fill. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate; PNS 16.

q: Which of these should NOT bear on a non-load-bearing masonry wall?
n: A non-loadbearing CHB wall is infill between columns and beams. Roof rafters must bear on the structural frame (beams or wall plates on columns). Cabinets and counters are light, attached loads. Source: NSCP 2015 Chapter 7 (masonry); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is the binder in mortar and grout?
n: Portland cement is the binder in both mortar (cement, sand and water) and grout (more fluid, sometimes with fine gravel). Lime is only an optional additive for workability. Source: ASTM C270 (mortar) and C476 (grout); Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: How many CHB are needed per square meter of wall?
n: One 8" × 16" CHB face plus joint is 0.20 × 0.40 m = 0.08 m², so 1 ÷ 0.08 = 12.5 blocks per square meter of wall. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (CHB area method).

q: How many concrete hollow blocks are needed for a fence measuring 3 meters by 10 meters?
n: Area = 3 × 10 = 30 m², and 30 × 12.5 CHB/m² = 375 pieces. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (CHB area method).

q: How many hollow blocks are needed for a 32 square meter wall, including 5% contingency?
n: 32 m² × 12.5 = 400 CHB, and 400 × 1.05 for 5% contingency = 420 pieces. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (CHB area method).

q: A solid concrete wall is 3.00 m wide, 3.00 m high and 0.10 m thick. Using a Class B mix (7.5 bags of 40 kg cement per m³), how many bags are needed?
n: Volume = 3.00 × 3.00 × 0.10 = 0.90 m³. Class B takes 7.5 bags of 40 kg cement per m³, so 0.90 × 7.5 = 6.75, rounded up to 7 bags. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate, Table 1-2.

q: Given a room with dimensions of 5.0 m x 5.0 m and a ceiling height of 2.4 m, with two windows measuring 1.0 m x 1.2 m each and one door measuring 2.0 m x 1.0 m, how many concrete hollow blocks (CHBs) are required to build the walls of the room?
n: Gross wall area = 4 sides × 5.0 m × 2.4 m = 48 m². Openings = 2 × (1.0 × 1.2) + (2.0 × 1.0) = 4.4 m². Net = 43.6 m², and 43.6 × 12.5 = 545 CHB. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (CHB area method).
